newsitem.title: BULGARIA: Party registration starts for Bulgarian elections.
newsitem.headline: Party registration starts for Bulgarian elections.

text.p: Bulgarian politicians queued outside the National Electoral Commission on Tuesday to register their parties for general elections on April 19.
The ex-communist Socialists won the last general election in December 1994 but lost support as economic crisis worsened.

The Socialist candidate suffered a decisive defeat in presidential elections last November, and party leaders gave into demands for early parliamentary elections last month after 30 days of mass street protests.

The first to register was the newly-formed Euro-Left, a coalition set up as an alternative to the Bulgarian Socialist Party, which last month bowed to pressure for early elections and agreed to leave power.
Electoral officials said 13 parties and coalitions had handed in registration documents by early afternoon and there was still a queue outside.
"It's normal to have a queue on the first day and on the last day," one official said. The Euro-Left was keen to be first in line because two other parties also wanted green ballot papers.

The main opposition Union of Democratic Forces (UDF), which also registered on Tuesday, has not yet reached agreement with two smaller allied parties on whether to put up joint lists, despite more than two weeks of talks.

The International Monetary Fund (IMF) and other donors suspended funding last year because of the Socialists' failure to carry out promised reforms, but an IMF delegation is now in Sofia discussing a new agreement with the interim government led by Sofia's respected UDF mayor Stefan Sofianski.
The IMF wants Bulgaria to set up a currency board, a restrictive fixed exchange rate regime which would drastically cut spending and prevent uncontrolled printing of banknotes.
The Socialist government had accepted the IMF's proposal but other economists have now reopened the debate, saying such drastic measures may not be necessary.

Opinion polls show the UDF winning a majority in the new assembly. The new government will inherit inflation estimated at 100 percent for February alone, a crumbling and illiquid banking system, and severe grain and fuel shortages.
Party registration closes on March 19. As well as the Euro-Left, another new party, the Liberal Democratic Alternative of former president Zhelyu Zhelev, is also expected to contest the elections.

Last month, President Petar Stoyanov vetoed changes to the electoral law approved by the outgoing parliament which would have lowered the threshold for parties to enter the legislature. It remains at four percent, which will keep many small parties out.
